1. The animation shows how paying extra each month shortens a mortgage. An illustrative character, Tessa, has a house and a grid of payment tiles, one per month. It uses "loan math at the Oct 8, 2026 survey rate".

2. The grid of monthly tiles grows in frames 1–3 until it covers the whole loan term. Frame 4 labels a payment of $2,828 on the 30-year loan and shows the loan ending after about 195 months, with the last tiles highlighted in gold. Frames 5 and 6 add extra payments, and the grid gets shorter. By frame 6 the loan finishes in 180 months, which is 15 years. That takes about $733 extra on top of the $2,216 required payment.

3. Paying more than the required amount pays the principal down faster, so the loan ends sooner. Here, $733 a month extra turns a 30-year loan into a 15-year payoff. The tiles stand for months of payments, and fewer tiles means fewer payments.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that extra payments can cut years off a loan. The labels "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast" tell viewers not to treat it as a prediction or a recommendation. It says nothing about investing the money instead, so it doesn't settle your question.

5. The animation showed the idea of extra payments shortening the loan through its picture and numbers, but it did not give advice. Any takeaway that you should pay extra is my own conclusion, not something the picture or text said.

For your own situation, the image can't tell you which is better. That depends on your mortgage rate compared with the returns you expect from investing, your emergency savings, and your other debts. You said you can just afford the 15-year payment. That suggests locking in the required 15-year payment and keeping a cash cushion may matter more than extra payments.
